notable_claims: The 'Fanny Hill' incident led to the formation or activity of CICA.
classification.summary: This item is a repost of a discussion regarding the Committee for Internet Academic Freedom (CICA) and the aftermath of the 'Fanny Hill' controversy. It serves as a pointer to discussions occurring in newsgroups focused on electronic freedom and censorship.
classification.title: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

identity.subject: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

notable_claims: CICA's README file explicitly prohibits software containing political, religious, or sexually explicit content.
The site moderator has discretion to deem files 'unsuitable' for the archive.
classification.summary: Jon Noring critiques the content policy of the CICA anonymous FTP site at Indiana University. He argues that the site's refusal to host software containing political, religious, or sexually explicit material constitutes censorship. The dispute was triggered by CICA's refusal to archive a Windows-only adaptation of the literary work 'Fanny Hill'.
classification.title: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

identity.subject: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

notable_claims: The archivist at macarchive.umich.edu claimed MacPGP was illegal and therefore instructions for its use were inappropriate to host.
classification.summary: A user reports that the archivist at macarchive.umich.edu refused to host a guide on using MacPGP. The refusal was based on the claim that providing instructions for the program was inappropriate because the software was considered illegal.
classification.title: macarchive.umich.edu censors my guide!

notable_claims: macarchive.umich.edu refused to archive information/guides related to PGP.
classification.summary: A user reports that macarchive.umich.edu refused to archive a guide on how to use PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) on Macintosh systems. The author expresses frustration over the censorship of information regarding encryption software and requests other sites to host the guide.
classification.title: macarchive.umich.edu censors my guide!

notable_claims: The administrator claimed that including MacPGP in the archive was illegal.
classification.summary: A University of Michigan archive administrator refuses to host a guide for MacPGP, claiming that distributing the software is illegal. A responding user criticizes this stance as lacking rebelliousness and humility. The exchange highlights the tension between institutional compliance and the push for cryptographic freedom during the 'Crypto Wars'.
classification.title: Re: "Here's How to MacPGP!" guide.

notable_claims: Faculty should be free of institutional censorship
Academic freedom does not require neutrality
classification.summary: This item is a repost of a statement regarding academic freedom for faculty in Canada. The document asserts that faculty should be free from institutional censorship and clarifies that academic freedom does not necessitate neutrality.
classification.title: A Canadian statement on Academic Freedom

identity.subject: A Canadian statement on Academic Freedom

notable_claims: Academic freedom does not require neutrality on the part of the individual.
Academic members are entitled to freedom in research, publishing, teaching, and criticizing their own university.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shared a policy statement from the Canadian Association of University Teachers (CAUT) regarding academic freedom. The document asserts that academic freedom is essential for teaching, scholarship, and research, protecting members from institutional censorship regardless of doctrine. It emphasizes that academic freedom allows for commitment rather than requiring neutrality.
classification.title: A Canadian statement on Academic Freedom

identity.subject: A Canadian statement on Academic Freedom

notable_claims: Newsgroups at McGill U. were not going to be arbitrarily removed.
classification.summary: A forwarded message clarifies that newsgroups at McGill University were not going to be arbitrarily removed. This appears to be a response or correction to previous claims of censorship on the university's Usenet access.
classification.title: Decision made to arbitrarily censor Usenet at McGill

identity.subject: Re: Decision made to arbitrarily censor Usenet at McGill

notable_claims: The university was carrying 4,400 newsgroups and facing disk space shortages.
The decision to audit groups was initially perceived as a unilateral move by a single staffer without academic or librarian oversight.
The Senate Committee on Computing (SCC) is the formal body advising McGill on computing and networking matters.
classification.summary: A dispute arose at McGill University after a staff member announced an audit to delete Usenet newsgroups of 'questionable value' due to disk space constraints. David Jones characterized this as arbitrary censorship, while Director Alan Greenberg defended it as necessary resource management and promised the issue would be discussed by the Senate Committee on Computing (SCC).
classification.title: Decision made to arbitrarily censor Usenet at McGill

identity.subject: Re: Decision made to arbitrarily censor Usenet at McGill

notable_claims: The CICA archive selection policy allegedly incorporates viewpoint discrimination.
The policy falsely suggests that the University of Indiana and CICA do not archive religious material.
classification.summary: A repost discussing the archive selection policy of the CICA (Computer and Information Center Archive). The author argues that the policy falsely implies a refusal to archive religious material and introduces illegal viewpoint discrimination into its selection process.
classification.title: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

identity.subject: Re: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

notable_claims: Prohibiting 'prejudiced or discriminatory' messages in university archives may constitute illegal viewpoint-based discrimination.
University policies are sometimes used as facades to rationalize the personal doctrinal disapproval of archivists.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the CICA archivist's policy of refusing software containing political, religious, or discriminatory messages. He argues that such restrictions constitute illegal viewpoint-based discrimination and suggests the archivist is misrepresenting university policy to justify personal disapproval. The post includes a curated list of legal precedents regarding public forums and free expression.
classification.title: Re: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

identity.subject: Re: More on CICA (the fallout from Fanny Hill)

notable_claims: Acadia University deleted all alt.sex groups from its active reading list as of 01/28/94.
classification.summary: A report indicates that Acadia University in Canada removed all 'alt.sex' newsgroups from its active reading list on January 28, 1994. This action represents an instance of institutional content filtering on campus networks during the early era of Usenet.
classification.title: Censoring of news groups

notable_claims: Acadia University removed alt.sex groups from its active reading list as of January 28, 1994.
classification.summary: Michelle Crocker, a student at Acadia University, reports that the university deleted all 'alt.sex' newsgroups from its active reading list. She seeks information on whether universities have the legal authority to remove specific newsgroups based on subject matter.
classification.title: Censoring of news groups
